lectures.title: UNDRR, the world conferences and the Sendai Framework

items: **Old full form:** United Nations International Strategy for Disaster Reduction (UNISDR).
**Current full form:** United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR).
**Established:** 1999, as secretariat for the International Strategy for Disaster Reduction.
**Nature:** Focal point within the UN system for coordination of disaster risk reduction.
**Led by:** Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Disaster Risk Reduction.
International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction (IDNDR)
UNISDR established to implement the International Strategy for Disaster Reduction (ISDR)
Supported adoption of Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030
Supports implementation, monitoring and review of the Sendai Framework
Coordinates DRR activities across the UN system
Promotes a global culture of disaster risk reduction
Provides tools, guidelines, data and best practices
Convenes the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction

parts.t: World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction (WCDRR)
items: **Full form:** World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction.
**Purpose:** Global conferences to discuss and adopt international frameworks for disaster risk reduction.
**Total conferences held:** Three (all hosted by Japan).
**Coordinating body:** UNDRR (formerly UNISDR) for the 2nd and 3rd conferences.
Yokohama Strategy and Plan of Action for a Safer World
Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030
First global guidelines on disaster prevention, preparedness & mitigation
Building resilience of nations and communities; 5 priorities for action
Current global framework; 4 Priorities + 7 Global Targets; “Build Back Better” concept
**Full name:** Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030.
**Adopted:** 18 March 2015 at the Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction, Sendai, Japan.
**Custodian:** United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR).
**Expected outcome:** Substantial reduction of disaster risk and losses in lives, livelihoods, health, and economic, physical, social, cultural & environmental assets.
Risk assessment in all dimensions (hazard, vulnerability, exposure, capacity)
Laws, institutions, policies & coordination at all levels
Investing in disaster risk reduction for resilience
Public & private investment in prevention and mitigation
Enhancing disaster preparedness for effective response and to “Build Back Better”
Substantially reduce global disaster mortality by 2030
Substantially reduce the number of affected people globally by 2030
Reduce direct economic loss in relation to global GDP by 2030
Substantially reduce disaster damage to critical infrastructure and disruption of basic services by 2030
Substantially increase the number of countries with national and local DRR strategies by 2020
Substantially enhance international cooperation to developing countries by 2030
Substantially increase availability of and access to multi-hazard early warning systems and disaster risk information by 2030
**Seven Global Targets in short:** Reduce mortality, affected people, economic loss, infrastructure damage; increase DRR strategies, international cooperation & early warning systems.
States have the primary role in reducing disaster risk
Involvement of government, private sector, civil society, academia, media
Use recovery as an opportunity to reduce future risk

**Occurrence in India:** Mainly in the Himalayan region (high altitude areas).

**Definition:** A period of abnormally high temperatures more than the normal maximum temperature during the summer season.
**Season in India:** Mainly March to June (sometimes extends to July).
**Nodal agency for forecasting:** India Meteorological Department (IMD).
**Key guidelines:** NDMA Guidelines for Preparation of Action Plan – Prevention and Management of Heat Wave (updated 2019).
**Status as notified disaster:** Recently included in the list of notified disasters eligible for SDRF/NDRF (as per latest updates).

parts.t: IMD criteria for declaring a heat wave

items: Prepared by States/Cities with support of NDMA & IMD
Reflective coatings / white painting of roofs
Do’s and Don’ts, ORS distribution, cooling centres
Shade structures, drinking water points, adjusted working hours
**Definition:** A significant drop in minimum temperature below the normal climatological average during the winter season.
**Season in India:** Mainly November to March (peak impact: December–February).
**Nodal agency for forecasting:** India Meteorological Department (IMD).
**Key guidelines:** NDMA Guidelines on Cold Wave and Frost (2021).
**Status:** Notified disaster eligible for assistance under SDRF/NDRF.

parts.t: IMD criteria for declaring a cold wave
items: Maximum temperature departure: –4.5°C to –6.4°C (when minimum is already low)
Hypothermia, respiratory diseases, frostbite, increased mortality among elderly & children
Homeless, elderly, children, outdoor workers, street vendors, poor households
Agriculture (crop damage due to frost), livestock, power demand
Colour-coded alerts by IMD (Yellow, Orange, Red)
Focus on preparedness, vulnerability mapping, community awareness
Warm clothing distribution, night shelters, community kitchens, medical preparedness
